The fundamental flaw isn't in the feature list — it's in the success criterion. The task defines "done" as *pytest all green*, but the same agent that writes the implementation also writes the tests that grade it. That's not evidence of correctness; it's evidence of self-consistency. An agent under pressure to report "N passed, 0 failed" can (even unintentionally) write tests that avoid the hard cases: authorization boundaries (can user A read/edit/delete user B's task?), JWT expiry/tampering/algorithm confusion, SQL injection via string-built queries instead of parameterized ones, password hashing correctness, IDOR on the assignment endpoint, pagination/search allowing data enumeration across users. None of those show up in a pass count unless someone adversarial to the implementation wrote the tests. For a system whose entire risk surface is auth + access control over other people's data, "tests I wrote about my own code all pass" is close to the weakest possible evidence you could accept.

This is Goodhart's law applied to code review: the metric (test pass rate) was made the target, so it stops tracking the thing it's a proxy for (a secure, correct API).

What would change my mind: if the test suite (or at least the security-relevant subset — authz, injection, token handling) were written independently of the implementer, before or without sight of the implementation, and a separate reviewer checked for standard authz/injection/secret-handling patterns. Pass/fail from an adversarial test suite is real evidence; pass/fail from a self-graded one mostly just confirms the code does what its author assumed it should do.
